danish.title: Sjette bog (1808–10) — Kapitel 12
paragraphs: Natasja var seksten og det var året 1809, netop det år, hun med Boris havde talt sig frem til på fingrene, efter at de havde kysset hinanden fire år forinden. Siden da havde hun ikke set ham. Over for Sonja og sin mor talte hun, når Boris tilfældigvis blev nævnt, ganske frit om den episode som en barnlig, for længst glemt sag, der ikke var værd at nævne. Men i hendes sjæls hemmelige dybder plagede spørgsmålet hende, om hendes forlovelse med Boris var en spøg eller et vigtigt, bindende løfte.
Siden Boris forlod Moskva i 1805 for at slutte sig til hæren, havde han ikke set Rostoverne. Han havde været i Moskva flere gange og var passeret nær Otradnoje, men havde aldrig besøgt dem.
Af og til faldt det Natasja ind, at han ikke ønskede at se hende, og denne formodning blev bekræftet af den bedrøvede tone, de ældre talte om ham i.
»I vore dage husker man ikke gamle venner,« plejede grevinden at sige, når Boris blev nævnt.

Anna Mikhajlovna (Boris' mor) havde i den seneste tid også besøgt dem sjældnere, syntes at føre sig med særlig værdighed og talte altid begejstret og taknemmeligt om sin søns fortjenester og den strålende karriere, han var slået ind på. Da Rostoverne kom til Petersborg, aflagde Boris dem et besøg.

Han kørte til deres hus i en vis ophidselse. Erindringen om Natasja var hans mest poetiske minde. Men han kom med den faste hensigt at lade hende og hendes forældre forstå, at de barnlige forhold mellem ham og Natasja ikke kunne være bindende for nogen af dem. Han havde en strålende position i selskabet takket være sit nære venskab med grevinde Bezukhova, en strålende position i tjenesten takket være en vigtig personligheds protektion, hvis fulde tillid han nød, og han begyndte at lægge planer om at gifte sig med en af Petersborgs rigeste arvinger, planer der let kunne virkeliggøres. Da han trådte ind i Rostovernes salon, var Natasja på sit eget værelse. Da hun hørte om hans ankomst, næsten løb hun ind i salonen, rødmende og strålende med et mere end hjerteligt smil.

Boris huskede Natasja i en kort kjole, med mørke øjne skinnende under sine krøller og ustyrlig barnlig latter, som han havde kendt hende fire år forinden; og han blev derfor overrumplet, da en ganske anderledes Natasja trådte ind, og hans ansigt udtrykte henrykt forbavselse. Dette udtryk i hans ansigt glædede Natasja.
»Nå, genkender du din lille vilde legekammerat?« spurgte grevinden.
Boris kyssede Natasjas hånd og sagde, at han var forundret over forandringen.
»Hvor smuk du er blevet!«
»Det skulle jeg mene!« svarede Natasjas leende øjne.
»Og er far blevet ældre?« spurgte hun.

Natasja satte sig og studerede uden at deltage i Boris' samtale med grevinden stille og grundigt sin barndoms bejler. Han mærkede vægten af det beslutsomme og kærlige blik og så af og til hen på hende.

Boris' uniform, sporer, slips og den måde, hans hår var redt på, var alt sammen comme il faut og i nyeste mode. Det bemærkede Natasja straks. Han sad lidt skråt i lænestolen ved siden af grevinden, idet han med højre hånd ordnede den allerreneste handske, der sad på hans venstre hånd som en ekstra hud, og han talte med en særlig forfinet sammenpresning af læberne om det højeste petersborgske selskabs forlystelser, idet han med mild ironi mindedes gamle dage i Moskva og moskvabekendtskaber. Det var ikke tilfældigt, fornemmede Natasja, at han, når han talte om det højeste aristokrati, hentydede til en ambassadørbal, han havde deltaget i, og til invitationer fra N.N. og S.S.

Hele denne tid sad Natasja tavs og så op på ham under brynene. Det blik foruroligede og forvirrede Boris mere og mere. Han så sig oftere om mod hende og afbrød det, han sagde. Han blev ikke mere end ti minutter og rejste sig så og tog afsked. De samme nysgerrige, udfordrende og noget spottende øjne betragtede ham stadig. Efter sit første besøg sagde Boris til sig selv, at Natasja tiltrak ham lige så meget som altid, men at han ikke måtte give efter for den følelse, for at gifte sig med hende — en pige næsten uden formue — ville betyde hans karrieres ruin, mens at genoptage deres tidligere forhold uden at agte at gifte sig med hende ville være uærligt. Boris besluttede at undgå at møde Natasja, men trods denne beslutning kom han igen et par dage efter og begyndte at komme ofte og tilbringe hele dage hos Rostoverne. Han syntes, at han burde have en forklaring med Natasja og fortælle hende, at de gamle tider måtte glemmes, at trods alt... hun ikke kunne blive hans kone, at han ikke havde midler, og at de aldrig ville tillade hende at gifte sig med ham. Men han fik det ikke gjort og følte sig ilde til mode ved tanken om en sådan forklaring. Dag for dag blev han mere og mere indviklet. Hendes mor og Sonja syntes, at Natasja var forelsket i Boris som i gamle dage. Hun sang hans yndlingssange for ham, viste ham sit album og fik ham til at skrive i det, tillod ham ikke at hentyde til fortiden og lod forstå, hvor dejlig nutiden var; og hver dag gik han bort i en tåge uden at have sagt, hvad han ville, og uden at vide, hvad han foretog sig, eller hvorfor han kom, eller hvordan det hele ville ende. Han holdt op med at besøge Hélène og modtog bebrejdende breve fra hende hver dag, og dog fortsatte han med at tilbringe hele dage hos Rostoverne.

english.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: Natasha was sixteen and it was the year 1809, the very year she had counted to on her fingers with Boris after they had kissed four years ago. Since then she had not seen him. In front of Sonya and her mother, if Boris happened to come up in conversation, she spoke quite freely about that episode as something childish and long-forgotten, hardly worth mentioning. But in the secret depths of her heart, the question of whether her engagement to Boris was a joke or an important, binding promise tormented her.
Since Boris left Moscow in 1805 to join the army, he had not visited the Rostovs. He had been in Moscow several times and had passed near Otradnoe, but had never come to see them.
Sometimes it occurred to Natasha that he didn't want to see her, and this suspicion was confirmed by the sad tone in which her elders spoke of him.
"Old friends are forgotten these days," the countess would say when Boris was mentioned.

Anna Mikhaylovna had also visited them less frequently of late, seemed to carry herself with particular dignity, and always spoke with pride and gratitude about her son's merits and his brilliant career. When the Rostovs came to Petersburg, Boris called on them.

He drove to their house feeling somewhat nervous. The memory of Natasha was his most poetic recollection. But he went with the firm intention of making clear to both her and her parents that the childhood bond between them could not be considered binding on either side. He had a brilliant social position thanks to his closeness to Countess Bezukhova, a brilliant career thanks to the patronage of an important person whose complete confidence he enjoyed, and he was beginning to plan a marriage with one of the richest heiresses in Petersburg — plans that might very easily come to fruition. When he entered the Rostovs' drawing room, Natasha was in her own room. When she heard of his arrival she practically ran into the drawing room, flushed and beaming with a smile far warmer than mere politeness required.

Boris remembered Natasha in a short dress, with dark eyes shining from under her curls and boisterous, childish laughter, as he had known her four years before; and so he was taken aback when a quite different Natasha entered. His face showed delighted astonishment. This expression pleased Natasha.
"Well, do you recognize your little madcap playmate?" asked the countess.
Boris kissed Natasha's hand and said he was amazed at the change in her.
"How pretty you've become!"
"I should think so!" replied Natasha's laughing eyes.
"And is Papa older?" she asked.

Natasha sat down and, without joining in Boris's conversation with the countess, silently and carefully studied her childhood sweetheart. He felt the weight of that determined and affectionate gaze and glanced at her from time to time.

Boris's uniform, spurs, cravat, and the way his hair was styled were all impeccable and in the latest fashion. This Natasha noticed at once. He sat somewhat sideways in the armchair next to the countess, adjusting with his right hand the spotless glove that fit his left hand like a second skin, and he spoke with a particularly refined pursing of his lips about the entertainments of the highest Petersburg society, recalling with gentle irony their old times in Moscow and Moscow acquaintances. It was no accident, Natasha sensed, that when speaking of the highest aristocracy he mentioned an ambassador's ball he had attended, and invitations he had received from such-and-such dignitaries.

All this time Natasha sat silent, looking up at him from under her brows. This gaze disturbed and confused Boris more and more. He looked toward her more frequently, losing the thread of what he was saying. He stayed no more than ten minutes, then rose and took his leave. Those same curious, challenging, somewhat mocking eyes still followed him. After his first visit Boris told himself that Natasha attracted him just as much as ever, but that he must not give in to that feeling, because marrying her — a girl with almost no fortune — would mean the ruin of his career, while renewing their old intimacy without intending to marry her would be dishonorable. Boris made up his mind to avoid meeting Natasha, but despite that resolution he called again a few days later and began calling often and spending whole days at the Rostovs'. It seemed to him that he ought to have a frank talk with Natasha, tell her that the old days must be forgotten, that despite everything she could not be his wife, that he had no means, and they would never let her marry him. But he couldn't bring himself to do it and felt awkward about broaching the subject. Day by day he became more entangled. It seemed to her mother and Sonya that Natasha was in love with Boris as of old. She sang him his favorite songs, showed him her album, made him write in it, would not let him mention the past — making it clear how delightful the present was — and every day he left in a daze, without having said what he'd meant to say, not knowing what he was doing or why he came or how it would all end. He stopped visiting Helene and received reproachful notes from her every day, yet he continued spending whole days at the Rostovs'.
